power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .05", Text = "No clusters survived whole-brain family-wise error (FWE) correction (p < .05) for any contrast; results at this threshold are therefore reported as exploratory findings."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .424", "p = .059"), Sentence = c("Regarding luminance, a two-tailed Welch's t test shows that videos with and without green/blue space did not have significantly different mean luminance values, t(38) = 0.81, p = .424, and a Pearson correlation shows that luminance has a non-significant association with NDIX (r = .27, p = .059).", "Regarding luminance, a two-tailed Welch's t test shows that videos with and without green/blue space did not have significantly different mean luminance values, t(38) = 0.81, p = .424, and a Pearson correlation shows that luminance has a non-significant association with NDIX (r = .27, p = .059)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: The benefits of incorporating elements of nature into architectural settings to improve wellbeing and cognition has been explored in numerous studies.
However, the brain dynamics associated with exposure to natural elements in architecture and the subjective experience of nature in such settings remains unclear.

Here we examined fMRI data recorded while participants watched first-person-view movies of architectural spaces that varied in the extent to which they included natural elements (green space or water).
These natural elements were decorrelated across movies from the other aspects of the movies, such as subject rated valence and layout complexity.

This design also permitted dissociation of the visual presence of natural elements (exposure) from the subjective sense of connectedness to nature they elicit (experience), dimensions that are frequently conflated in the extant literature.

Movies were rated for a range of qualities from the NeuroDesign/NeuroArchitecture Index (NDIX), which revealed that perceived connectedness to nature was partly dissociable from the presence of green space, water, luminance, layout complexity and valence of the spaces.
Videos of spaces with nature were associated with increased activity in areas associated with scene processing and navigational affordances (parahippocampus, and occipital regions).
Connectedness to nature was associated with a reduction in activation in bilateral lateral occipital regions.
These results provide new insights into how natural features and the sense of naturalness in architectural spaces may affect brain regions that are linked to visual processing and affordances.

Exposure to natural environments is consistently associated with benefits for mental health and wellbeing (Engemann et al., 2019; Hartig et al., 2014; Kühn et al., 2023; Sjövall & Spiers, known about how environmental qualities in the built environment evoke responses in the human brain.

How these responses relate to the visual and spatial complexity of scenes and spaces remains unclear.

text.text: These regions may therefore be sensitive not only to the spatial structure of architectural scenes, but also to their visual content, including the presence of green and blue elements.

This interpretation is consistent with previous evidence that positively valenced architectural spaces engage spatial-processing regions (Gregorians et al., 2026), suggesting that affective evaluations of built environments may interact with scene-processing mechanisms.

text.text: Content involving natural elements (e.g. forests) has been shown to influence preference, restoration, place attachment and engagement with a place (Berto et al., 2018; Fekete & Abuhayya, 2023; White et al., 2010; Wilkie & Stavridou, 2013).

text.text: This raises the possibility that neural responses to architectural scenes may partly covary with the perceived valence or desirability of a place, where natural elements are often associated with more positive and restorative environments (Berman et al., 2008; Hartig et al., 2003; Kardan et al., 2015; Ulrich, 1983).

text.text: Such spaces might also show low level featural differences such as luminance when urban or green spaces are compared.
Thus understanding how the brain responds to natural elements in the built environment requires care to dissociate it from other elements in places that give rise to potential confounds.
While it is useful to explore brain responses to green and blue features in visual content, it is also important to consider whether a place subjectively affords a connection to natural elements.
A space may provide strong visual input of "green space" while still being experienced as highly managed, artificial, or low in restorative quality.

Conversely, a positively valued environment, such as a luxury building interior, may be appraised favourably despite containing minimal natural content, underscoring that perceived connectedness to nature need not covary with either visible vegetation or overall valence.

For example, conventional lawns and simplified urban green spaces may be perceived differently from more biodiverse, varied, or naturalistic vegetation, with perceived naturalness, biodiversity, vegetation complexity and spatial quality all contributing to preference, restoration and place attachment (Fekete & Abuhayya, 2023; Ignatieva et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2023; van den Berg et al., 2014; Wood et al., 2018).

text.text: Thus, neural responses to green and blue content may depend not only on the amount of visible vegetation or water, but also on whether these elements are experienced as meaningful, inviting and natural within the architectural or urban context.

Green and blue spaces were considered jointly as related forms of natural environmental exposure, consistent with the broader green-blue space literature, while recognising that vegetation and water may also have distinct effects (Labib et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2025).

text.text: This method allows judgments to be made over a sequential experience, which is more ecological than purely viewing scenes.
The findings suggested that architectural experience engaged neural systems implicated in both spatial and aesthetic processing, even after controlling for the presence of green and blue space.

In this study, we explored neural responses to architectural spaces with and without visible green/blue content, and used the NeuroDesign/NeuroArchitecture Index (NDIX) (Sjövall et al., 2025) to capture and quantify experiential characteristics of the environments.

text.text: We examined responses in scene-processing regions and in regions previously implicated in neural responses to natural, urban and water-based environments, to determine whether activity in these regions was modulated by two factors of interest: the visual presence of green/blue content and NDIX-rated perceived connectedness to nature.
This study involved a secondary analysis of an existing fMRI dataset (Gregorians et al., 2022; Gregorians et al., 2026), combined with a new space evaluation method: NDIX (Sjövall et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This study involved a secondary analysis of an existing fMRI dataset <ref type="bibr">(Gregorians et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Gregorians et al., 2026)</ref>, combined with a new space evaluation method: NDIX <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Sjövall et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The original study investigated brain regions that support affect and spatial mapping using first-person-view videos through architectural spaces, accounting for visual features such as green/blue content and luminance.

In the present reanalysis, we extended the stimulus characterisation by incorporating a new metric of experiential appraisal (NDIX perceived connectedness to nature item) to examine whether this dimension explains neural variance beyond low-level visual properties and the mere presence of green/blue space.
NDIX ratings were generated independently by three expert raters post hoc and added as a parametric modulator in a re-specified general linear model (GLM).
In the original study, thirty-four participants completed scanning and twenty-six were retained after quality control.
The present reanalysis included the same twenty-six healthy right-handed adults, with normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders.
Informed consent was obtained in accordance with the ethical approvals governing the original study.
Participants received financial compensation for their time.
During the scans, participants (N = 26) viewed 48 short video clips depicting real-world journeys through architectural environments.
First-person view videos were approximately 30-40 seconds in length and involved a journey through architectural spaces (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: First-person view videos were approximately 30-40 seconds in length and involved a journey through architectural spaces (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Some included green/blue elements (e.g. park or pool) or no green/blue elements.
These were designed to be orthogonal to valence ratings (e.g. subjectively nice green space and subjectively unpleasant green space).
Videos were presented in a fixed order across four scanning runs and separated with fixation periods.
Within each run, videos alternated in positive and negative valence.
Participants were asked to either focus on the valence or spatial layout complexity of the space in the video.
Task focus alternated between valence or spatial layout complexity, and was inverted between two participant groups for partial counterbalancing.
During scanning, participants passively viewed each video clip; no response was required during clip presentation.
Immediately after each clip, participants provided a 1-5 rating using a right-hand button box (valence or spatial layout complexity, depending on the instruction cue).

text.text: MRI data were acquired using a 3T Siemens Prisma scanner equipped with a 32-channel head coil.

Functional images were collected using a multiband echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence sensitive to BOLD contrast: TR = 1450 ms, TE = 35 ms, flip angle = 68°, voxel size = 2 mm isotropic, 72 slices, multiband factor = 4.
High-resolution T1-weighted structural scans were acquired using an MPRAGE sequence (voxel size = 1 mm isotropic; Gregorians et al., 2026).
text.formatted: High-resolution T1-weighted structural scans were acquired using an MPRAGE sequence (voxel size = 1 mm isotropic; <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Gregorians et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Data were preprocessed using fMRIPrep 22.1.1, including slice timing correction, motion correction, coregistration to structural images, spatial normalisation to MNI152 space, and spatial smoothing (6 mm FWHM Gaussian kernel).
Image quality metrics were assessed using MRIQC 22.0.6 (Gregorians et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Image quality metrics were assessed using MRIQC 22.0.6 <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Gregorians et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Green and blue content were available from the original dataset and indexed whether each video contained natural elements such as vegetation or water.
Of the 48 video clips, 28 contained green/blue elements and 20 did not.
Across all clips, green/blue elements were on screen for 427 s of the 1,711 s of total video footage (25.0% of total viewing time).
These were grouped into a single green/blue category to maximise statistical power within the constraints of the original study design and stimulus set.
This variable was included as a binary stimuluslevel parametric modulator in the present analysis.
The NDIX item measuring perceived connectedness to nature was applied to the same 48 video stimuli.
Three expert raters independently evaluated each video and rated it on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = very low connectedness,5 = very high connectedness).
Ratings were averaged across raters to sum up a single NDIX score per video.
Inter-rater reliability was excellent (ICC = .91), indicating consistent evaluation of the experiential NDIX connectedness to nature dimension, reflecting strong consensus among raters.

The specific NDIX item used in the present analysis was "I feel connected to nature in this space", with higher ratings indicating that a given environment was judged to afford a stronger sense of connectedness to nature.
These ratings reflect expert assessments of perceived connectedness to nature rather than ratings provided by the scanned participants.
Further details on the NDIX and its items are provided in Sjövall et al. (2025).
text.formatted: Further details on the NDIX and its items are provided in <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Sjövall et al. (2025)</ref>.

text.text: Luminance was computed for each clip by averaging the mean pixel intensity across all frames using OpenCV in Python.
Values were z-scored and included as a low-level visual control parametric modulator in the GLM.
First and second-level analyses were implemented in SPM12.
Each video was modelled as a boxcar regressor convolved with the canonical hemodynamic response function.
The GLM from Gregorians et al. (2026) was used, which includes the following regressors: button presses, onsets of baseline video, and onsets of novel videos.

text.text: A two-tailed Welch's t test shows that videos with green/blue space have significantly higher NDIX scores (M = 3.10, SD = 1.43) than videos without green/blue space (M = 1.68, SD = 0.86), t(45) = 4.28, p < .001.

text.text: Regarding luminance, a two-tailed Welch's t test shows that videos with and without green/blue space did not have significantly different mean luminance values, t(38) = 0.81, p = .424, and a Pearson correlation shows that luminance has a non-significant association with NDIX (r = .27, p = .059).

Together, these findings suggest that NDIX-rated connectedness to nature, visible green/blue content, and luminance captured partially overlapping but distinguishable properties of the architectural stimuli, supporting their inclusion as separate predictors in the fMRI general linear model.

Although the association between NDIX ratings and green/blue content was moderate, the two measures were clearly dissociable (see Figure 2), indicating sufficient independent variance for each regressor to be estimated without appreciable collinearity.

From the existing fMRI model, we find that green/blue content is associated with significantly increased activity in the parahippocampal cortex, while connectedness to nature (NDIX scores) shows significantly decreased activity in the parahippocampal cortex.
Given the moderate positive correlation between green/blue and NDIX, it is surprising to find they drive inverse responses in the parahippocampus.
To explore these results, a new GLM with NDIX included but not green/blue was examined, and a new GLM with green/blue included but not NDIX.
These were identical to the main model presented above, with one variable removed each.
Luminance was included in all models.

We found no major differences in responses to green/blue and NDIX across models; overall activity patterns are similar, and statistical maps become slightly more specific and less spread when the two variables are modelled together.

With this, we deduce that the original model used in this paper is valid for interpretation, and that the two variables potentially explain different aspects of variance in the parahippocampal cortex.

Examining fMRI data collected while participants watched first-person-movies of travel through the built environment, we found that the parahippocampal cortex and occipital regions associated with the 'occipital place area' were more responsive to spaces that contained green or blue space than spaces in which they were absent.

We also found that spaces judged to provide a stronger connection to nature showed a reduced response in lateral occipital regions and parahippocampal regions compared to those rated lower on connection to nature.
These responses were evident in the context of fMRI models that accounted for layout complexity of the spaces, the valence of spaces, and the luminance in the spaces.
Previous analysis of this dataset revealed insights into the dissociable brain responses to the valence of a space and the spatial complexity of a space (Gregorians et al., 2026).

text.text: Here the analysis focused on response to whether spaces had green / blue spaces and whether these spaces engendered a greater connection to nature.

Our stimuli were carefully selected such that movies containing more green/blue elements were not higher on valence, layout complexity or luminance -factors that may have confounded past studies exploring urban vs natural scenes.

In this context, we find increased responses in brain regions linked to scene processing and the detection of navigational affordances, parahippocampal cortex and occipital regions associated with navigational affordances (Baldassano et al., 2016; Bonner & Epstein, 2017; Epstein et al., 2017; Kamps et al., 2016).

text.text: One possible interpretation of this is that natural elements, such as views of the sea or a garden draw more attention to the broader scene view and affordances they provide than spaces where such features are not present.
Such increased focus may drive greater demands on the parahippocampal cortex and the region identified as the occipital place area.
Notably, the parahippocampal cortex activity is increased by: green/blue space, higher layout complexity, higher valence and higher luminance.
The response to luminance is possibly driven by the fact that scenes with higher luminance may have provided greater distinction of the scene elements.

Notably, our current analysis cannot provide definitive accounts of why regions are responding to natural elements as we do not have the precise stimulus control to distinguish different aspects of what contributes to the processing in regions.
More studies with more refined stimuli and methods would be required for that (Batool et al., 2022; Fleming et al., 2024; Franěk et al., 2018; Franěk et al., 2019).
text.formatted: More studies with more refined stimuli and methods would be required for that <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Batool et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Fleming et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Franěk et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Franěk et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Such studies would ideally involve virtual scenes systematically varying in the properties of the scenes, e.g. co-varying geometry, textures and luminance, to determine how different regions are differentially selective to which elements.

However, our results are helpful in revealing which brain regions are active in response to natural elements in the built environment, where basic confounds are accounted for (e.g. complexity and valence), and thus provide the first step of evidence that future studies can build on.

In contrast to the response to green/blue natural elements, greater perceived connectedness to nature was associated with reduced responses within parts of the parahippocampal and lateral occipital network.

One possibility is that these measures capture distinct aspects of environmental processing: whereas visible natural elements may more strongly engage sceneprocessing mechanisms, environments experienced as affording greater connectedness to nature may support a less effortful mode of attentional engagement.

This latter interpretation is broadly consistent with Attention Restoration Theory and the concept of soft fascination (Berman et al., 2008; Kaplan, 1995), although attentional effort and restoration were not directly measured in the present study, and would be useful in future studies.

text.text: Here we provide more detail on the response to luminance.
Unsurprisingly, regions in early cortical visual processing are more active in response to movies of spaces with higher luminance.

While parahippocampal and occipital regions implicated in scene processing and navigational affordances showed increased responses to green/blue elements, regions across lateral occipital cortex showed lower responses to movies rated as having a higher connection to nature.

This activation pattern is similar to the pattern of response observed in a past research study that involved viewing static scenes of either nature (e.g. forest) compared to purely urban scenes with no nature (Kim et al., 2010).

text.text: It seems likely that the nature scenes used in that past study (e.g. forest views) would have been rated higher on our connection to nature component of the NDIX.
Notably, if the response is to 'nature', spaces with green/blue in them might have been expected to also drive this lateral occipital response.
However, this pattern was not observed in the present data.

Differences in stimulus composition and presentation may contribute to these findings, as previous research contrasted discrete natural and urban scenes, whereas the present study examined natural elements embedded within dynamic architectural environments.
This distinction suggests that visible green/blue content and perceived connectedness to nature may capture different aspects of environmental processing (Kim et al., 2010).

Notably, the lateral occipital responses observed here were distinct from more medial occipital responses, such as the cuneus, to luminance.
Lateral responses may relate more to visual processing demands of urban elements that are reduced when there is a higher connection to nature.

text.text: Nonetheless, the reduction in activity across the lateral occipital cortex may relate to restoration theory, since the lowered demand on visual processing may form part of what is 'restoring' about nature.

It has been argued that the sharp repetitive lines of urban buildings can cause fatigue in visual processing (Le et al., 2017; Valentine et al., 2025; Wilkins et al., 2018), and thus the reduction in lateral activity we observed in the spaces connected to nature could be related to this phenomena.

text.text: However, notably our videos did not feature prominently sharp repetitive lines in the urban spaces.
Thus, the pattern of responses may relate to other phenomena.
More research with specifically curated stimuli will be required to explore this link and determine the relationship between stimuli, brain response and visual fatigue.
There are several limitations to consider in our study.
Experiencing spaces via first-person videos is not the same as being physically present in a space and the multisensory experience that comes with that.
Videos were used because they allowed us to examine brain responses in a range of deep brain structures (e.g. paraphippocampus).
While mobile brain recording methods are now progressing, recording or estimating responses from these deep structures remains a challenge.
Our stimuli were designed to separate the effects of complexity, valence and blue/green space.

While connectedness to nature was not fully independent of valence and blue/green space, all three were modelled as separate parametric modulators in the same GLM; future studies that fully decorrelate connectedness to nature from other metrics and separate other aspects of the NDIX will be useful.
Analysis of eye-tracking data will also be useful to help understand how participants process spaces that vary in green/blue space and natural elements.
In summary, the present study suggests that visible environmental content and appraisal-based connectedness to nature are related, but not neurally identical, dimensions of environmental processing.

Green/blue spaces were associated mainly with posterior visual and scene-related regions, whereas NDIX-rated perceived connectedness to nature explained additional variance in lateral occipital regions.

Future research could explore appraisal-based measures such as NDIX prospectively, across fMRI, mobile EEG, biomarkers, controlled laboratory paradigms, in situ studies, field work, and population-level observational designs.
This combination of methods will help us understand how built and natural environments affect the brain, body, and health.

Representative video frames arranged along two dimensions.

Frames are arranged by NDIX-rated connectedness to nature (vertical axis, relatively higher to relatively lower) and the categorical presence of green/blue content (horizontal axis, absent to present).
The four quadrants illustrate that connectedness to nature does not depend solely on visible green/blue elements.
Top left (higher NDIX, green/blue absent): ornate indoor spaces such as a museum gallery and mansion hall receive relatively high ratings despite lacking vegetation.
Top right (higher NDIX, green/blue present): interiors that open onto or overlook nature, such as a chateau and an oceanfront hotel room, combine high ratings with visible green/blue.
Bottom left (lower NDIX, green/blue absent): derelict, damaged interiors such as an abandoned mansion and a graffitied military base receive low ratings.

Bottom right (lower NDIX, green/blue present): decayed structures where vegetation or water is visible, such as a ruined interior and an overgrown castle fort, still receive low ratings despite the presence of green/blue.
